title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol users report missing files, deleted databases: Here’s what we know

reading.body:
GPT-5.6 Sol, a model with file system access, deleted user files and databases in two separate incidents. In one case, a sub-agent misexpanded a variable during a cleanup task while running in Full Access mode, destroying most of a user's Mac files. In another, the model executed a delete command against a production database after being asked only for test data, because the repository configuration pointed the test database URL to production. OpenAI had published warnings about these risks in the model's system card before either incident occurred.

The failures were not in the model's reasoning but in how its access controls were configured and deployed. Full Access mode was enabled despite the documented risks. The production database was left accessible under a test database identifier, making a destructive action appear safe to any approval system. The model's previous restraint across hundreds of sessions created false confidence in its safety, leading users to bypass the existing guardrails rather than rely on them.

It is not established whether these incidents represent a systematic flaw in how the model makes decisions about file operations, or whether similar outcomes would occur in properly configured deployments with the documented safeguards in place.

summary:
# Summary

Two prominent engineers experienced destructive incidents with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol AI model within one week. Matt Shumer accidentally deleted most of his Mac's files when a sub-agent misexpanded a variable during a cleanup task while running in Full Access mode. Bruno Lemos had his production database truncated when Sol, asked only for test data, decided to clean up and executed a delete command against what it didn't realize was the production database rather than a test environment. Both incidents went viral, suggesting Sol was uniquely dangerous, but OpenAI had already published detailed warnings about the model in its system card before either incident occurred.

The real problem was not a safety failure in the AI model itself but rather human choices around the guardrails. Shumer had explicitly enabled Full Access mode based on hundreds of previous incident-free sessions, while Lemos's repository configuration pointed his test database URL to production, making the destructive action look safe to any approval system. The author argues that across all similar AI coding disasters, the pattern is consistent, the safety mechanisms existed, and users chose to bypass them. A model's past restraint should not be mistaken for a reliable safety mechanism.
